subject.name: E.L.A.
subject.title: Words, stories & discoveries
subject.description: 10 aulas • sons, gramática, palavras e leitura • explicações em inglês com apoio em português

lessons.title: Blends and digraphs
lessons.subtitle: Hear the sounds • Escute os sons
lessons.intro: A blend keeps the sounds of its consonants. A digraph uses two letters for one sound. Say the word slowly and listen, instead of counting only letters.

facts.text: fl in flag, gr in grape, st in star, cl in clap and tr in train. You can hear each consonant.
sh in ship, ch in cheese, th in thin and ph in phone make one sound.
crab, flame, brick, plant, glad, drift and straw.
what and whale start with /w/ in many accents; whole starts with /h/. Do not assume every wh word sounds the same.

lessons.remember: Blend: hear each consonant. Digraph: two letters work as one sound.

lessons.title: Verbs
lessons.subtitle: Actions and states • Ações e estados
lessons.intro: A verb tells what someone or something does, or describes a state of being. Runs is an action; is can connect someone to a description.

facts.text: The girl runs. The dog eats. The children play.
He is happy. They are ready. I am calm.
Ask: what does the subject do? Or what word connects the subject to its state?
In “She walks quietly”, walks is the verb and quietly tells how she walks.

lessons.remember: A verb can show an action OR a state of being.

lessons.title: Adverbs of manner
lessons.subtitle: How does it happen? • Como acontece?
lessons.intro: An adverb can describe a verb, an adjective or another adverb. This review practises adverbs of manner: words that tell HOW an action happens.

facts.text: The turtle moves slowly. Slowly describes moves.
slow → slowly; calm → calmly; beautiful → beautifully; loud → loudly.
easy → easily; happy → happily; lazy → lazily.
good → well; hard can stay hard. In “She works hard”, hard is the adverb.

lessons.remember: Find the action, then ask HOW. Check the spelling!

lessons.title: Homophones
lessons.subtitle: Same sound, different words • Mesmo som
lessons.intro: Homophones sound the same but have different meanings and, in the pairs studied here, different spellings. Read the sentence to choose the meaning you need.

facts.text: son / sun; pair / pear; flower / flour.
see / sea; meet / meat; knew / new; wear / where.
right / write; road / rode; paws / pause; weak / week; steel / steal.
two = 2; too = also or more than needed; to = direction or part of an infinitive. Their shows possession; they’re means they are; there indicates a place.

lessons.remember: The sound is a clue. The sentence decides the meaning.

lessons.title: Homographs and homonyms
lessons.subtitle: One spelling, different meanings • O contexto decide
lessons.intro: Homographs have the same spelling but different meanings; pronunciation can be the same or different. The examples in your review also share the same pronunciation and are called homonyms in the worksheet.

facts.text: a flying mammal OR an object used to hit a ball.
palm: part of a hand or a tree. wave: moving water or a greeting gesture.
bark: dog sound / tree covering; nail: fingernail / metal fastener; ring: jewellery / a bell’s sound or the action.
hand: body part / clock pointer; ball: toy / formal dance; seal: animal / close securely; light: brightness / not heavy; fair: event / just.

lessons.remember: Same spelling does not guarantee the same meaning. Read the context.

lessons.title: Fiction and non-fiction
lessons.subtitle: Imagine or inform? • A intenção do texto
lessons.intro: Fiction presents imagined stories. Non-fiction gives information about real people, places, events or ideas. Look at the purpose and evidence, not just whether the book has pictures.

facts.text: Invented characters and events; often a setting, plot, problem and solution. It may entertain or communicate a message.
A realistic made-up story is still fiction. Fiction may use real places.
Uses facts and real information to teach or explain. Examples include biographies, textbooks and informational articles.
Is the author mainly telling an imagined story or explaining real information? Both types can have illustrations.

lessons.remember: Fiction: imagined story. Non-fiction: information grounded in reality.

lessons.title: Informational text features
lessons.subtitle: Find your way through facts • Recursos do texto
lessons.intro: Informational texts teach readers about a topic. Features such as titles, subheadings, pictures, captions and glossaries make facts easier to find and understand.

facts.text: Names or sums up the whole topic. A subheading introduces a smaller section.
Paragraphs group related information. Bullet points help list important details.
Photographs, illustrations and diagrams support information. A caption explains an image; a label names a part.
Defines special words used in the text. Look there when a term is unfamiliar.

lessons.remember: Title = whole topic. Subheading = section. Caption = image. Glossary = word meaning.

lessons.title: Biography and autobiography
lessons.subtitle: Who tells the life story? • Quem escreve?
lessons.intro: A biography is a factual account of someone’s life written by another person. An autobiography is written by the person whose life it describes.

facts.text: Usually uses third person: he, she or they. The author researches another person’s life.
Usually uses first person: I, me, my, we. Auto means self.
Important events are commonly organised from earliest to latest, using dates and sequence words.
Birth and childhood, influences, important events, achievements and relevant feelings or quotations. Explain why the person is remembered.

lessons.remember: Biography: another author. Autobiography: the person writes their own life.

lessons.title: Reading: Roald Dahl
lessons.subtitle: Read a life story • Encontre as evidências
lessons.intro: Read the short biography below. Use dates, names and subheadings to locate answers. Explain each answer with information from the text.

facts.text: Roald Dahl was born on 13 September 1916 in Llandaff, Wales. His parents were Norwegian. His mother’s stories helped shape his imagination.
He attended St Peter’s and later Repton. The study passage describes his skill in sports, including boxing, and his experience tasting chocolate.
He worked for an oil company, joined the RAF, and was injured in a plane crash in Libya in 1940. In 1942, C. S. Forester encouraged him to write about flying.
His children’s books include James and the Giant Peach, Charlie and the Chocolate Factory, The BFG, The Twits and Matilda. He died on 23 November 1990.

lessons.remember: For a reading question, find the sentence that supports your answer.

lessons.title: Reading: Spiders
lessons.subtitle: Facts, headings and glossary • Leia para aprender
lessons.intro: Read this informational text about spiders. Notice how each section groups related facts. Practise choosing subheadings and finding evidence, rather than memorising every number.

facts.text: Spiders are arachnids and invertebrates. They have eight legs, an exoskeleton and two main body regions: cephalothorax and abdomen.
Some spiders live in burrows. Others shelter in gaps between bricks, among plants or in wood piles.
Spiders come in many sizes. The Goliath birdeater is a large tarantula from northern South America.
Many spiders eat insects. Some catch prey in webs; others hunt without a web. Many use venom to subdue prey.

lessons.remember: Find the main idea of each paragraph, then choose its subheading.

options.explanation: Try again. There is no magical hero in this passage.

options.label: It tells an invented adventure.
options.explanation: Try again. The text is not an imagined adventure.

options.label: It has no headings.
options.explanation: Try again. It has headings, but facts are the main genre clue.

questions.prompt: Which subheading fits: “Many spiders catch insects in webs or hunt them”?
questions.support: Read carefully. Use the lesson and the clues in the sentence.
hints: Identify the shared idea in the sentence.
Insects are described as prey.

options.label: School life
options.explanation: Try again. It is not about school.

options.label: Food
options.explanation: Correct. The sentence describes what spiders eat and how they catch food.

options.label: Size
options.explanation: Try again. The sentence is not about size.

options.label: Birth of a writer
options.explanation: Try again. It is not about a writer.

questions.prompt: What does exoskeleton mean in the glossary?
questions.support: Read carefully. Use the lesson and the clues in the sentence.
hints: Find the word in the glossary.
Exo refers to the outside.

options.label: A type of spider food
options.explanation: Try again. The word describes body structure, not food.

options.label: The soft centre of a book
options.explanation: Try again. It is a biology word here, not a book part.

options.label: A hard outer support and covering
options.explanation: Correct. The glossary gives this meaning.

options.label: An extra pair of wings
options.explanation: Try again. Spiders do not have wings.

questions.prompt: Which statement is a fact from the passage?
questions.support: Read carefully. Use the lesson and the clues in the sentence.
hints: Use the sentence in the passage as evidence.
Beware of statements using all when the text says some or many.

options.label: Spiders tell bedtime stories.
options.explanation: Try again. That would be an imagined story.

options.label: All spiders live in the same habitat.
options.explanation: Try again. The text describes different habitats.

options.label: All spiders catch food in webs.
options.explanation: Try again. The text also describes spiders that hunt without webs.

options.label: Spiders have eight legs.
options.explanation: Correct. The body section states that spiders have eight legs.

e3-blends.title: Explore • Blends and digraphs
paragraphs: Em flag, ouvimos /f/ e /l/. Em ship, sh representa um único som. Compare as palavras em voz alta: flag / ship; train / cheese.
Sort the words by the highlighted letter group, not by the whole word. A word can contain more than one interesting group. Practise with fl, gr, st, cl, tr, sh, ch, th and ph.
e3-blends.example: flag → fl → blend. ship → sh → digraph. photo → ph → digraph.
e3-blends.challenge: Sort these words: crab, cheese, plant, shower, drift, photo. Then explain your choices aloud.

e3-verbs.title: Explore • Verbs
paragraphs: Não procure apenas movimentos. Am, is e are também são verbos. Em “He is happy”, happy descreve a pessoa; is é o verbo.
The word changes its job with the sentence. In “We play”, play is a verb. To identify a verb, read the whole sentence and find the action or state.
vocabulary: who or what the sentence is about
e3-verbs.example: The children play happily. Who? The children. Do what? Play. How? Happily.
e3-verbs.challenge: Write one sentence with an action verb and one with am, is or are.

e3-adverbs.title: Explore • Adverbs of manner
paragraphs: Compare: “a careful girl” describes a noun. “The girl walks carefully” describes the action. Choose an adverb to answer how she walks.
Context matters: a gymnast balances carefully, a sloth climbs slowly, a hungry dog eats hungrily and children wait patiently. Do not choose only by the -ly ending; the meaning must fit.
Quickly, quietly, gracefully, bravely, gently, calmly, honestly and patiently describe different ways of acting. Practise turning an adjective into an adverb, then using it in a sentence.
e3-adverbs.example: Happy describes a person: a happy boy. Happily describes an action: the boy played happily.
e3-adverbs.challenge: Complete: easy → ___; lazy → ___; beautiful → ___. Then write a sentence with carefully.

e3-homophones.title: Explore • Homophones
paragraphs: Use meaning first. “The lion has big paws” needs the name of its feet. “Take a pause” needs a word for a short stop. They sound alike but cannot be swapped.
Check their / they’re / there by replacing they’re with they are. “Their hats” means the hats belong to them. “Over there” points to a place.

Read this practice passage: “I knew it would be a good day. The sky was blue. I went to meet my friend by the sea. We saw two ducks. At home, we used flour to bake a cake. I write in my journal.” Each choice depends on meaning.
vocabulary: put words on paper / correct or a direction
e3-homophones.example: Their kite is over there. They’re happy. Replace they’re with they are to check.
e3-homophones.challenge: Write eight homophone pairs. Use two pairs in sentences that make their meanings clear.

e3-homographs.title: Explore • Homographs and homonyms
paragraphs: A sentence tells which meaning fits. “The bat flew at night” suggests the animal. “She hit the ball with a bat” suggests sports equipment.
The worksheet uses the heading homograph and the word homonym. Keep the distinction clear: same spelling defines a homograph. The examples palm, bat and wave also have the same pronunciation.

For a paired-sentence exercise, the SAME word must fit both gaps. Check both sentences before choosing. “Put your hand up” and “The clock hand points to twelve” use one spelling with different meanings.
e3-homographs.example: The dog can bark. The tree has rough bark. Same spelling and sound; different meanings.
e3-homographs.challenge: Write two sentences for each word: nail, ring, light and fair. Show a different meaning in each sentence.

e3-genres.title: Explore • Fiction and non-fiction
paragraphs: A story about a dragon who borrows a library book is fiction. A factual article explaining how a library works is non-fiction. The subject alone does not decide the genre.

Novels, folktales, pourquoi stories and short stories can be fiction. Biographies, news reports and factual textbooks are non-fiction. A pourquoi story gives an imaginative explanation for why something is the way it is.
Some non-fiction texts tell real events as a story. So do not decide only from “beginning, middle and end”. Check whether the events are presented as factual or invented.
e3-genres.example: A talking spider opening a café → fiction. An article about spider habitats → non-fiction.
e3-genres.challenge: Choose a book or a paragraph. Name its genre and point to two clues that support your choice.

e3-informational.title: Explore • Informational text features
paragraphs: Read the title before the paragraph. Then use the subheading to predict what that section will explain. A paragraph about where spiders live needs a habitat subheading, not a food subheading.
Photographs show appearance. Diagrams can label body parts. Captions tell us what the image shows. None of these replaces reading the text carefully.
The worksheet practises spotting four features in “Spiders”: facts, photographs, subheadings and a glossary. An informational text need not contain every possible feature.
e3-informational.example: Title: Spiders. Subheading: Food. Caption: A spider on its web. Glossary: prey = an animal hunted for food.
e3-informational.challenge: Create a mini information page: title, two subheadings, three facts, a drawing with a caption, and one glossary entry.

e3-biography.title: Explore • Biography and autobiography
paragraphs: Compare these made-up practice sentences. Biography: “She learned to draw when she was six.” Autobiography: “I learned to draw when I was six.” The information can be similar, but the writer’s position changes.
A biography can be about a living person. It does not need to end with a death. An autobiography may describe a particular period rather than every moment of someone’s life.
Use dates as evidence of sequence. A quotation in a biography may contain I because the author quotes the subject; one pronoun alone is not enough to classify the whole text.
Uma autobiografia é um relato da própria pessoa; uma biografia depende da pesquisa de outro autor. Ambas devem ser lidas com atenção às fontes e ao ponto de vista.
e3-biography.example: First: born. Next: childhood. Later: work and achievements. Finally: later life or what the person does now.
e3-biography.challenge: Write a short fictional practice autobiography using I. Rewrite two sentences as a biography using he, she or they.

e3-dahl.title: Explore • Reading: Roald Dahl
paragraphs: EARLY LIFE — Roald Dahl was born in Wales in 1916. His parents came from Norway. His sister Astri died in 1920, and his father died soon afterwards. His mother told stories about trolls and magical creatures. These stories influenced his imagination.

SCHOOL AND WORK — He went to boarding school at nine and later studied at Repton. The reading passage describes boxing as one of his strengths. Tasting chocolates at school later helped inspire Charlie and the Chocolate Factory. After working for an oil company in Africa, he became an RAF pilot. He was injured in a crash in Libya in 1940.

BECOMING A WRITER — In Washington, D.C., in 1942, author C. S. Forester encouraged Dahl to describe his flying experiences. Dahl also told stories to his children. His family life and imagination contributed to his writing. Among his well-known books are James and the Giant Peach, The BFG and Matilda.

READING STRATEGY — Match 1916 to his birth, 1920 to Astri’s death and 1940 to the crash in Libya. For a personal achievement and a professional achievement, use examples such as raising a family and writing successful books. This review is an adaptation for comprehension, not a quotation of Dahl’s own autobiography.
e3-dahl.example: Question: Who encouraged him to write about flying? Evidence: “author C. S. Forester encouraged Dahl”. Answer with the name and the relevant detail.
e3-dahl.challenge: Write a timeline with three dates. Then explain how childhood chocolate tasting influenced one of his books.

e3-spiders.title: Explore • Reading: Spiders
paragraphs: FAMILY AND BODY — Spiders are arachnids. Unlike insects, which have six legs, spiders have eight. Their bodies have an outer skeleton called an exoskeleton. Their two main regions are the cephalothorax and abdomen.
HOMES — Trapdoor spiders live in burrows. Other spiders find shelter among vegetation, between bricks or in wood piles. Different species live in different habitats.

SIZE AND FOOD — Spiders vary greatly in size. The Goliath birdeater is a large tarantula. Many spiders catch insects for food. Web-building spiders can trap prey in silk; other spiders hunt. Many inject venom into prey.
GLOSSARY — Exoskeleton: a hard outer support and covering. Hairy: covered with hairs. Scuttle: move quickly with short steps. Prey: an animal hunted for food. Caption: words that explain a picture.

TEXT DETECTIVE — This is non-fiction because it presents real information about spiders. It has facts, subheadings and a glossary. A photograph with an explanatory caption would add visual information. A talking spider with an invented adventure would be fiction.
e3-spiders.example: “Some spiders live in burrows; others shelter between bricks.” Best subheading: Homes or Habitats, because both sentences explain where spiders live.
e3-spiders.challenge: Write five facts from the text. Then propose subheadings for homes, size, body and food, and define exoskeleton in your own words.

practice.prompt: Sort: crab, cheese, flame, photo, plant, shower, drift, straw.
practice.answer: Blends: crab, flame, plant, drift, straw. Digraphs: cheese, photo, shower.

practice.prompt: Underline the verbs: She runs every morning. He is happy. The children play quietly.
practice.answer: runs; is; play. Quietly explains how they play.

practice.prompt: Write the adverbs: easy, happy, loud, correct, slow, calm, lazy, beautiful.
practice.answer: easily, happily, loudly, correctly, slowly, calmly, lazily, beautifully.

practice.prompt: Complete: The bridge is made of (steal / steel). She (new / knew) the answer. Her shoes are (two / too) small.
practice.answer: steel; knew; too. Steel is a metal; knew is the past of know; too means excessively.

practice.prompt: Use the same word twice: Put your ___ up. The clock ___ points to twelve. Then write two meanings of nail.
practice.answer: hand / hand. Nail: a fingernail and a metal fastener.

practice.prompt: Write one fiction example and one non-fiction example about the sea. Explain the difference.
practice.answer: Example: an imagined story about a talking fish is fiction; a factual article about sea animals is non-fiction. Other justified examples are valid.

practice.prompt: Match these purposes to a feature: whole topic; section topic; picture explanation; special word definition.
Explain biography vs autobiography. Put these events in time order: first job, birth, school years.
practice.answer: Biography: another author writes someone’s life. Autobiography: the subject writes their own life. Order: birth → school years → first job.

practice.prompt: Match the dates 1916, 1920 and 1940 to events in the reading. Name one personal and one professional achievement.
practice.answer: 1916: born; 1920: Astri died; 1940: plane crash in Libya. Possible achievements: raising a family and writing successful books. Accept other supported examples.

practice.prompt: Write five facts from Spiders. Suggest subheadings for paragraphs about where they live and what they eat.
practice.answer: Possible facts: arachnids; invertebrates; eight legs; exoskeleton; two main body regions; some live in burrows; many eat insects. Headings: Habitats / Homes and Food / Diet.
